seo.title: Altrazen — Software studio
seo.description: Altrazen is a software studio building web applications, SaaS products and mobile apps in TypeScript — and rescuing the codebases other people left behind.

hero.headline: Software built to be maintained.
hero.subheadline: We build web applications, SaaS products and mobile apps — and we take over the codebases that were shipped fast and now have to be safe to run.

positioning.heading: A studio that stays after launch
paragraphs: Most software fails slowly. It ships, it works, and then eighteen months later nobody can change it without breaking something, the person who understood the deploy has gone, and a rewrite starts to look cheaper than another patch.

We build to avoid that outcome, and we take on the systems where it has already happened. The two halves feed each other: reading other people's broken codebases is the best education there is in what not to do in your own.

points.title: We write for the next developer
points.description: Small pull requests, real documentation, and architecture decisions recorded with their reasoning. If only one person can maintain something, that is a defect we introduced.

points.title: Everything lives in your accounts
points.description: Repository, hosting, domains, store listings, monitoring — set up under your ownership from the first commit. Leaving us should never be technically difficult.

points.title: We say no early
points.description: If a project is too small for us, outside our stack, or would be better solved by not building software at all, you hear it on the first call rather than three weeks in.

capabilities.heading: Four things we do properly
capabilities.description: A short list we go deep on, rather than a long one we would be learning on your budget.

flagship.heading: The codebase nobody wants to touch
flagship.description: Software built fast — by a previous agency, a developer who left, or an AI coding tool — usually works and is usually unsafe. These are the findings that come up again and again when we open one.

findings.label: Secrets in the repository
findings.description: API keys and database URLs committed to git. Deleting them later does not help — the history keeps them.

findings.label: Backups that have never been restored
findings.description: An automated backup nobody has tested is a belief, not a backup.

findings.label: Authorisation in the browser
findings.description: Permission checks written in client code. Anyone who opens developer tools walks straight past them.

findings.label: Errors caught and discarded
findings.description: Failures swallowed with no logging and no alert. The application looks healthy while quietly losing writes.

findings.label: No way back
findings.description: Deploys go straight to production with no staging and no one-step revert, so a bad release becomes an emergency.

findings.label: Dependencies left behind
findings.description: Packages years out of date with published vulnerabilities, now far enough behind that upgrading is a project of its own.

steps.title: Talk
steps.outcome: You describe the problem. We tell you whether we are the right people, including when we are not.

steps.title: Scope
steps.outcome: A written proposal: what we will build, what we will not, the timeline, and the risks we can already see.

steps.title: Build
steps.outcome: Working software on a preview URL every week, in pull requests small enough to read, with a written update.

steps.title: Hand over or keep going
steps.outcome: Documentation and a walkthrough, then either your team runs it or we maintain it. Both are fine.

standards.heading: What we hold ourselves to
standards.description: These are not aspirations. Each one is a rule we apply on every engagement, and each one costs us something.

items.title: Nothing ships without a way back
items.description: Every deploy is reversible in one step, and we test the rollback before launch rather than during an incident.

items.title: Secrets never touch the repository
items.description: Not in any branch, not at any point in history. Where we inherit them, rotating and purging is the first thing we do.

items.title: Every alert reaches a person
items.description: An alert that only lands on a dashboard nobody opens is not monitoring. If it cannot wake someone, it does not count.

items.title: Tests where failure costs money
items.description: Payment, authentication and data writes get covered. We do not chase a coverage percentage — that optimises the number, not the risk.

items.title: Accessibility is a build requirement
items.description: WCAG 2.2 AA, keyboard paths tested by hand, checked in CI. Not a phase that gets cut when the date slips.

items.title: We tell you about our own mistakes
items.description: Immediately, in plain language, with what we are doing about it. Finding out later from your users is not an option we accept.

technologies.heading: Boring technology, chosen deliberately
technologies.description: One language across the stack and a short list of tools we know deeply. Everything we use has to be hireable, reversible, and observable in production.

whoWeAre.heading: Small, and growing on purpose
paragraphs: Altrazen is a small engineering studio. That is a deliberate size, not a stage we are trying to escape: it means the people who talk to you are the people writing the code, and nothing gets translated through an account manager who has never seen the repository.

It also means we take on fewer engagements at a time than a larger agency, and we turn down work that is not a fit. If you are looking for a team that will tell you when the answer is no, that is the trade.

finalCta.heading: Tell us what you're building
finalCta.description: Or what is already broken. One conversation is usually enough to know whether we are the right studio for it — and we will say so either way.
